doc.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Bandstand signals: 'five' for D flat, Bucky's eyebrows, Ray Brown's 'garbage'
summary: Pizzarelli explains cues like 'here we go' and always saying 'five' for D flat, a habit from Bucky. He describes his father's eyebrow signals and Ray Brown's 'garbage' cue for the China cymbal.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young

blocks.x: Well during the song it might be to — I might say like sometimes I say, “Here we go” and it means we’re finishing the song. Like we’ll be playing a tag [scats] “Here we go” [scats] and everybody knows. Sometimes I just say stupid things to him to make him laugh. So like between songs. Or I’ll just say we’re going to do this next and, you know and I’ll say like, “I almost did okay on that one” you know or something. Like trying to keep it a little lighter. But during the song sometimes I’ll yell out a new key, and the funny thing was, and two piano players, actually Isaiah and Tadataka Unno, a Japanese piano player, I always — if I want to call D flat as a key I say “five.” It’s an old Bucky thing, five flats is D flat. And it seems to me that I don’t do it for any other keys but D flat. I always say five. I won’t say four, A flat, is the A flat. But for D flat it’s always five. It’s been a Bucky thing forever. So one time at the very beginning of Isaiah’s time with us I turned around and said, “Let’s do ‘Body and Soul’ in five.” And Isaiah turned to Mike and said, “Wow, that’s sort of cool.” He said, “I think he means D flat.” And the © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

same thing, I think Tadataka said the same thing, he says, “You only say ‘five’ for D flat.” He goes, “It’s like one of those weird things.” Because we trade fours I’ll say “fours.” But “five” is D flat. It’s one of those little communication things. When I was with Bucky it was always eyebrows were the communicator. So when you’re playing, if you’re playing this way and you look over and you saw him go like that it meant he was going to look at you, or in that case me, and I knew something — here there’s a change that’s coming and the eyebrows always signaled that.

I just, that’s so interesting. And I’ve seen it. I’ve probably done it myself, but the look, like you get this look and with guitar players, you know there’s the hand, and the look should tell you what this is going to be. And you go, “Well that could be lot of things.”

Yeah. But since we’ve been playing together they know that that means they know what the section is. It’s like with Bucky I knew when his eyebrows went up, okay he’s going to either turn it over to me or here comes the shout chorus or something of that, that was the message. I know that there’s a couple of things, somebody wrote the other day, it was Ray Brown’s birthday and somebody wrote — oh George Fludas the drummer put up a thing that was Ray, George Fludas and Larry Fuller at the piano and Fludas had gone to his, there’s a certain cymbal, the China cymbal. And he’s playing away on it and the signal from Ray was, “Garbage.” ‘Cause he said it was a garbage lid. That cymbal. So he’d say, “Go garbage” something, just say “garbage” and he knew that’s the cymbal that Ray wanted.
Was there such a thing in a jazz group as like five sharps, or jazz guys don’t play in five sharps, but rock guys do.
